name: Moodfit
summary: Mood tracking and CBT-based mental health app with highly rated tools for depression, anxiety, and stress self-management.
description: Moodfit is a mental health app focused on helping you track your mood, understand what affects it, and build healthier habits over time. It combines mood tracking, CBT-based thought records, gratitude, sleep and exercise tracking, and symptom questionnaires (like PHQ-9 and GAD-7) to support people dealing with depression, anxiety, and everyday stress.
patient_summary: Moodfit is like a fitness app but for your mental health. You track your mood, sleep, exercise, and thoughts, then the app shows patterns and suggests tools like CBT exercises, gratitude journaling, and breathing to help you feel better. It’s best for people who want to understand their moods and actively work on them. It is not a replacement for therapy or medication if your symptoms are severe.

citation.title: Usability evaluation of a mobile mood tracking application (Moodfit)

clinical_trials.outcome: In a lab-based usability study with 14 participants, the Moodfit app was found to be effective, efficient, and reliable-in-use for tracking mood and related factors. Several usability issues were also identified that, if fixed, could further improve engagement and performance.

linked_conditions.context: Daily mood tracking, behavioral activation goals, and PHQ-9 monitoring can support treatment for depression when used alongside therapy or medication.
CBT-based thought records and breathing/mindfulness tools may help reduce worry and tension in mild to moderate GAD as a self-help supplement.
Long-term tracking of mood, activity, and sleep can help people and their clinicians see patterns over months and years.
Daily mood and sleep tracking can support bipolar treatment by helping track early warning signs and medication effects, but only when supervised by a clinician.

contraindications: Not a substitute for professional mental health treatment, diagnosis, or crisis services.
Not appropriate as the sole intervention for moderate to severe depression, active suicidal ideation, or psychosis.
People with bipolar disorder should only use mood tracking apps as part of a treatment plan with a clinician, not for self-diagnosis.
May increase distress if used for constant self-monitoring in people who are highly self-critical or obsessive about symptoms.

efficacy_data.comparison_data: No randomized controlled trials of Moodfit’s clinical efficacy have been published yet.
efficacy_data.patient_text: There are no formal clinical trials showing how much Moodfit improves depression or anxiety symptoms. The app uses evidence-based tools (like CBT exercises and mood tracking), but its specific impact hasn’t been measured in controlled studies.

exclusions: Active suicidal ideation or self-harm behavior
Moderate to severe major depressive episodes without professional care
Manic episodes or untreated bipolar I disorder

data_collected: Email address and basic account information
Mood ratings and tags (what affects your mood)
Usage data (which tools you use, how often)
Optional: PHQ-9 and GAD-7 questionnaire responses
Optional: Sleep, exercise, and habit logs

privacy_rating.certification: No formal third-party privacy certification disclosed; app states that data are encrypted and not disclosed to outside parties except as necessary for payment processing.

sections.heading: What Moodfit Does
sections.text: Moodfit is designed to help you understand and improve your mental health the way a fitness app helps with physical health. You rate your mood each day, add what might be influencing it (sleep, exercise, caffeine, social contact, work, etc.), and track patterns over time. The app then offers CBT-based tools like thought records, gratitude journaling, breathing exercises, and goal setting to help you build habits that support better mood and resilience.

sections.heading: How Well Does It Work?
sections.value: Effective and efficient in usability testing
sections.comparison: No controlled symptom outcome trials yet
sections.text: A small usability study with 14 participants found that the Moodfit app was effective, efficient, and reliable-in-use for completing core tasks like logging mood, tracking habits, and reviewing insights. Participants were able to complete tasks successfully and generally felt that the app helped make mood tracking and reflection easier. However, this study did not directly measure changes in depression or anxiety symptoms, and no formal randomized controlled trials of Moodfit’s clinical impact have been published yet.
sections.patient_text: Moodfit appears easy to use and helpful for tracking how you feel and what affects your mood. There’s not yet strong research showing exactly how much it improves depression or anxiety, but it uses tools (like CBT and mood tracking) that have good evidence in general.

sections.heading: Who Should Use Moodfit?
sections.text: Moodfit is best for people who:
items: Want to understand patterns in their mood over days, weeks, and months.
Are dealing with mild to moderate depression or anxiety and want to actively work on habits and thoughts between therapy sessions.
Like data and graphs that show how sleep, exercise, medication, and activities affect their mood.
Want a single place to track PHQ-9 or GAD-7 scores over time and share trends with a clinician.
Prefer practical CBT-style tools (thought records, behavioral activation, gratitude, self-care) over long guided meditations.
Are motivated to check in most days and log their mood, even when they’re not feeling great.
not_recommended: People with severe depression, active suicidal thoughts, or recent suicide attempts who need urgent, professional care.
People with psychosis (hallucinations, delusions) who need close clinical supervision and medication.
People with bipolar disorder using mood tracking without clinician guidance, as it may increase anxiety or rumination about symptoms.
Anyone who finds daily self-monitoring makes them more self-critical or obsessively focused on symptoms.
People who want a mostly passive, entertainment-style app (Moodfit is more like a workbook and dashboard than a relaxation app).

items.description: Rate your mood on a scale and add tags for what might be influencing it (sleep, work, caffeine, social connection, medication, etc.). Over time, Moodfit builds charts that show how habits and life events correlate with mood changes.
items.evidence: Mood tracking can help people with depression and anxiety notice triggers earlier and see the impact of positive behaviors, especially when combined with therapy.

items.description: Fill out standard depression (PHQ-9) and anxiety (GAD-7) questionnaires regularly and track scores over time. You can export this information to share with a therapist or doctor.
items.evidence: PHQ-9 and GAD-7 are widely used, validated tools for screening and monitoring depression and anxiety symptoms in clinical practice.

items.description: Guided exercises help you identify automatic negative thoughts, examine evidence for and against them, and create more balanced, helpful thoughts.
items.evidence: Thought records are a core tool in cognitive behavioral therapy with strong evidence for reducing depressive and anxious thinking when used consistently.

items.description: Daily prompts and tracking for gratitude, enjoyable activities, and meaningful actions. Helps shift attention toward positive experiences and reinforce behavioral activation.
items.evidence: Gratitude and behavioral activation exercises have been shown to improve mood and reduce depressive symptoms in multiple studies.

items.description: Track sleep duration, exercise, and other habits alongside mood to see relationships (e.g., worse mood after short sleep, better mood after exercise).
items.evidence: Consistent sleep and regular exercise are strongly associated with better mental health and lower risk of depression and anxiety.

items.description: Set reminders to log your mood, take medication, practice gratitude, or complete self-care activities. Track progress toward personalized goals.
items.evidence: Reminders and clear goals make it easier to build and maintain new health habits over time.

sections.heading: Privacy & Data Security
sections.summary: Moodfit states that user data are encrypted, not sold, and not disclosed to outside parties except for essential services like payment processing. Grade: A-
items: Encryption of stored data and communications with the server.
No sale of personal data to advertisers or data brokers.
Limited sharing of information with payment processors for subscriptions.
Mood and symptom data kept private to the user unless they choose to export and share it.
Users can export their data to share with a therapist or doctor.
data_collected: Usage metrics (which tools are used, how often).
data_shared: Payment and subscription information with app store or payment providers.
Aggregated or de-identified analytics data may be used internally to improve the app.
concerns: Any app that stores sensitive mental health data could be a concern if a device or account is compromised.
Even de-identified data, if combined with other sources, might theoretically be re-identified, though the app does not state that it shares data for advertising purposes.
Moodfit is not a HIPAA-covered product and should not be used as an official medical record.
sections.hipaa_note: Moodfit is not HIPAA-compliant and is not intended to store protected health information in the way an electronic health record does. If you share app data with your clinician, ask how they will store and protect it.

sections.heading: How to Start Using Moodfit
steps: Download Moodfit from the Apple App Store or Google Play Store.
Create an account with your email and set a secure password.
Complete the onboarding questions about your goals (e.g., depression, anxiety, stress, general wellbeing).
Set up daily mood tracking and choose factors (sleep, exercise, medication, social contact) you want to track.
Optionally complete baseline PHQ-9 and GAD-7 questionnaires so you can track symptom changes over time.
Explore tools like CBT thought records, gratitude, and breathing exercises, and pin a few favorites.
Set reminders so that checking in with your mood becomes a consistent daily habit.
tips: Try to log your mood at roughly the same time each day so patterns are easier to see.
Add notes or tags when something significant happens (big event, medication change, major stressor).
Share exported reports with your therapist or doctor so they can see how your mood and symptoms have changed between visits.
Start small: focus on tracking just a few things (mood, sleep, one habit) instead of everything at once.
Use CBT and gratitude tools on days when your mood is low, not just when things are going well.
common_mistakes: Only logging mood when you feel terrible (this makes it harder to see positive patterns or improvements).
Expecting the app alone to treat moderate or severe mental illness without professional help.
Trying to track too many factors at once and getting overwhelmed.
Forgetting to update the app for weeks and then assuming it “doesn’t work.”
Using scores (like PHQ-9) to self-diagnose instead of as a conversation starter with a clinician.

items.comparison: Daylio is another mood tracking and journaling app that uses icons and short entries. It’s simpler and more lightweight than Moodfit, but has fewer CBT-style tools and symptom questionnaires.
Headspace focuses more on guided meditation and mindfulness training rather than detailed mood tracking. Good if you want structured meditation courses instead of data-heavy self-monitoring.
Calm is better for sleep and relaxation (Sleep Stories, music) and less focused on mood data and CBT tools. Moodfit is a better fit if you like charts and active mental fitness exercises.

faqs.a: Moodfit is used to track your mood, understand what affects it, and practice tools like CBT exercises, gratitude, and behavior tracking to support your mental health. It’s aimed at people dealing with depression, anxiety, stress, and low motivation who want a structured way to work on their mental fitness.

faqs.q: Is Moodfit clinically proven to work?
faqs.a: Moodfit itself does not yet have large randomized controlled trials showing how much it improves depression or anxiety symptoms. A small usability study found that the app was effective and efficient to use, but did not measure symptom change. The app uses evidence-based components like CBT thought records, mood tracking, and behavioral activation, but its specific impact has not been formally quantified.

Moodfit offers a free tier with core mood tracking and some tools. Additional features and deeper insights require a paid subscription, usually available as monthly or annual plans. Exact pricing depends on your country and app store.

faqs.q: Can Moodfit replace therapy or medication?
faqs.a: No. Moodfit is a self-help and tracking tool, not a replacement for therapy or medication. It can be very helpful alongside treatment—for example, tracking mood between sessions and doing CBT exercises—but it should not be relied on as the only support if you have significant depression, anxiety, or other mental health conditions.

faqs.q: Is Moodfit good for bipolar disorder?
faqs.a: Mood tracking can be extremely useful in bipolar disorder to spot early warning signs and sleep changes, but it should only be used under the guidance of a psychiatrist or therapist. Moodfit is not a diagnostic or treatment tool for bipolar disorder and should not be used on its own to manage mood episodes.

faqs.q: Can I share Moodfit data with my therapist?
faqs.a: Yes. Moodfit allows you to export your data (such as mood charts, PHQ-9 and GAD-7 scores, and habit tracking) so you can share them with your therapist or doctor. This can make appointments more efficient by showing what has been happening between visits.

According to available information, Moodfit states that it does not sell users’ personal data. Data are encrypted and shared only as needed with services like payment processors. As with any app, you should review the most current privacy policy before sharing sensitive information.

faqs.q: Who should not use Moodfit on its own?
faqs.a: People with severe depression, active suicidal thoughts, recent suicide attempts, psychosis, or severe bipolar episodes should not rely on Moodfit alone. They need urgent evaluation and ongoing care from mental health professionals. Moodfit can sometimes be added later as a supplement, with guidance, once safety and basic treatment are in place.

faqs.q: How often should I use Moodfit to see benefits?
faqs.a: Moodfit works best when used consistently. Many people aim to log their mood once or twice a day and use at least one tool (like a CBT thought record, gratitude exercise, or habit tracking) several times per week. The value comes from building up enough data to see patterns and from practicing skills regularly.

faqs.q: Is my data secure in Moodfit?
faqs.a: Moodfit reports that it uses encryption to protect user data and does not sell personal information. However, like any app, it is not a HIPAA-covered medical record system. Use a strong, unique password, enable device security (PIN, biometrics), and be cautious about where and how you share exported data.
